Core Compounders|U|Universe: Chris Hohn states that leaving out banks, airlines, wireless telecom, media and ad agencies means avoiding what he calls bad businesses, because they face heavy competition or, for banks, high leverage, so profits are fragile. A mentioned example: air travel grew about 5% a year for a century, yet airlines collectively made minimal profits. Pat Dorsey states that excluding industries like airlines, auto parts, life insurance and oil and gas means avoiding price takers, because a large part of their future is not under their control. No specific past example given. Terry Smith states that dropping low-return sectors makes sense because good-company sectors don't become bad ones and vice versa; low-return industries stay low. A mentioned example: the airline industry, which he says never makes an adequate return on capital.
Core Compounders|G1|History: Dev Kantesaria states that a long record matters because a company only meets his bar for predictability if he is confident it stays dominant for at least the next 10 years, and he prefers business models that have already worked for decades. No specific past example given. Chris Hohn states that a long history is informative because "good companies stay good and bad companies stay bad": barriers to entry persist, though only if you judged quality right in the first place. No specific past example given.

Core Compounders|G4|Consistent profits: Dev Kantesaria states that steady profits signal predictability, which he will not give up, because he hates losing money and avoids anything that "could go down 90% tomorrow"; quality means growth and predictability together. A mentioned example: young software firms are too unpredictable, while Nestlé or Hershey are predictable but too slow. Threshold set at 2 loss years in 10 (Oct 2026): a deliberate loosening; the downturn rule (G9) still catches cyclical losers.
Core Compounders|G5a|High returns (media: Pat Dorsey states that a high return on capital for many years is the sign of a moat, because Morningstar's moat work started by studying every company earning over 15% on capital for over 15 years (numbers he calls arbitrary). He warns ROIC can mislead where investment is expensed. No specific past example given. Terry Smith states that a high return on capital is "the single most important thing", because over a long hold your return converges on what the business earns. A mentioned example: Munger's point that a business earning 6% on capital for 40 years returns about 6% even if bought at a huge discount.
Core Compounders|G5b|High returns (consi: Terry Smith states that returns held year after year signal lasting quality, because "Good companies don't become bad companies by and large or vice versa". A mentioned example: in data back to 1966, high-ROE companies stayed clustered around 20%, still well above the low-return group decades later. Pat Dorsey states that returns that keep holding up show a moat at work, because a moat lengthens the time before returns on capital decline to the cost of capital, so the company can keep reinvesting at high rates. No specific past example given.
Core Compounders|G6|Growth: Dev Kantesaria states that growth is half of quality, because a predictable company growing only 2-3% a year does not deliver strong long-term returns; he wants faster growth that is still predictable. A mentioned example: Nestlé and Hershey, which he calls extremely predictable but slow-growing. Pat Dorsey states that a reinvestment runway matters, because a company with an obvious place to put its cash is less likely to make a dumb acquisition or a badly timed buyback. A mentioned example: eBay, a great network-effect moat that ran out of room to grow once it had its market. Terry Smith states that growth is needed to reinvest cash at high returns, because high returns are wasted if the company is "landlocked" in a small niche or geography. No specific past example given.
Core Compounders|G7|Cash conversion: Terry Smith states that profits must turn into cash, because his first test of a good company is a high return on capital in cash: cash delivered in a period divided by capital employed. A mentioned example: he put his own portfolio at about 25% on this measure (2022). Connor Haley states that free cash flow is a better guide than reported profits, because earnings and EBITDA "can be easily manipulated". No specific past example given.
Core Compounders|G8|Balance sheet: Mala Gaonkar states that low debt matters because decent businesses she owned that were overlevered had much less room to maneuver when macro stress arrived; avoiding balance-sheet leverage, such as public LBOs, is one of her hard-learned lessons. A mentioned example: she names one such holding, spelled "Altis" in the captions, without further detail. Paul Singer states that surviving comes first, because big losses wreck judgment while intact capital lets you act in a crisis: "you make a buck you keep it". A mentioned example: he lost 88% of his parents' money on margin in 1974; in late 2008, "everything got cheap" for those with capital left.
Core Compounders|Flag|Margin collapse: Pat Dorsey states that a moat shows up as returns that take a long time to fall to the cost of capital, so a sharp margin drop can mean the moat is weakening; but he warns margins can also fall because investment like sales and software development is expensed. No specific past example given.
Core Compounders|Flag|Revenue shrinking: Terry Smith states that shrinking revenue must be judged across the cycle, because he wants secular, not cyclical, growth: each peak and trough should be bigger than the last, though growth needn't come every year. Dev Kantesaria states that a volume drop is acceptable only if it is temporary, because a toll collector keeps raising prices and earns more when volume returns, while pricing to hide secular volume decline can backfire. A mentioned example: FICO's mortgage-score volume fell for years while it raised those prices 100% one year and over 40% the next.

Core Compounders|V|Valuation: Terry Smith states that judging quality before price is right, because investors spend almost all their effort on whether a stock is cheap and far too little on whether the business is high-grade, and long-run returns follow the business. A mentioned example: Munger's point that a business earning 18% on capital for 20-30 years wins even at an expensive-looking price. Dev Kantesaria states that price should not decide inclusion, because a great compounder's value growth overcomes overpaying by 10 or 15%, and precise valuation is "a silly exercise". A mentioned example: he bought S&P Global at $17.50 during the financial crisis; it is now over $500, compounding he says he never could have expected.
Core Compounders|J|Human / AI review: Pat Dorsey states that moat durability needs human judgment, because "you can't screen for switching costs"; whether customers find it hard to switch is learned by talking to customers, ex-employees and salespeople. No specific past example given. Peter Thiel states that durability, not growth, drives most of a company's value, because growth is easy to measure today while whether a company still exists in a decade is hard to quantify. A mentioned example: about three-quarters of PayPal's value as of 2001 came from cash flows in 2011 and beyond. Connor Haley states that the review must ask why the stock might be mispriced, "the most important question in the investment process", because smart analysts with the same information usually price a stock fairly. No specific past example given.
